abstract: |
  Learning-assisted mixed-integer optimization must translate predictive accuracy into useful solver interventions. We investigate supervised bipartite graph neural predictions as partial MIP starts for capacitated facility location. The procedure prioritizes rare predicted positive assignments, preserves the original feasible region, and delegates completion to Gurobi. Training uses 54 quality-screened original instances partitioned into 34 training, ten validation, and ten predictive-test parents, with seed 42 and 100 epochs. Six medium validation instances qualify a fixed guidance policy; six distinct medium instances subsequently compare unguided optimization, learned starts, and a support- and class-matched root-relaxation comparator under a 3,600-second budget. Predictive evaluation yields pooled F1 of approximately 0.6993 and average precision of 0.7745 across 5,536,400 binary targets, whose positive prevalence is approximately 0.0951 percent. Learned starts improve terminal relative gap on five of six optimization-test instances, with a median paired difference of -1.164 percentage points. The mean effect is substantially influenced by two instances; four learned-start runs and all control runs are right-censored. These observations support a favorable but limited development demonstration, not population-level significance or a general speedup claim. We retain negative pilot results, distinguish predictive and optimization test populations, and provide artifact-level reproducibility. Replication, controlled synthetic augmentation, and evaluation on hard instances remain necessary.

# Introduction

Capacitated facility location combines discrete facility decisions with allocation subject to capacity restrictions. Mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) provides a general framework for such decisions, but difficult instances may leave a substantial primal-dual gap after hours of computation. Repeated solution of a related problem family creates an opportunity to learn assignment patterns. The practical question is not merely whether those patterns are predictable: it is whether they improve a solver without compromising the mathematical problem or its certificates.

We examine this question using CFL instances from [MILPBench](https://github.com/thuiar/MILPBench). A graph neural network (GNN) predicts binary solution values from variable-constraint incidence and root-relaxation information. Selected predictions become native partial MIP starts. Unselected variables remain unspecified; the solver completes or rejects the candidate and continues on the original model. This differs from fixing variable bounds, imposing a predicted solution, or replacing branch-and-bound.

The principal research question is: **Can supervised bipartite GNN predictions improve fixed-budget optimization on unseen-in-fitting medium CFL instances when supplied as nonbinding partial starts?** We investigate an original-instance predictor and a class-aware start construction, comparing it with unguided Gurobi and a root-LP start matched on support size and positive count. Our contributions are a specified offline/online procedure, a leakage-controlled computational comparison, and evidence that retains exclusions, regressions, measurement boundaries, and censored runs. The start construction is an operational heuristic, not a new optimality theorem. The small development benchmark does not establish general effectiveness across all CFL instances.

![Offline learning and online solver application. Training labels are unavailable to online inference; validation qualifies the policy before optimization-test execution. Partial starts leave the feasible region unchanged.](figures/figure_pipeline.pdf){#fig-pipeline width=100%}

# Related work

## Learning to Optimize

Learning to Optimize (L2O) exploits experience over problem distributions to improve components of optimization algorithms. @bengio2021 emphasize this distributional perspective and the distinction between learning an expensive decision and replacing a complete solver. @chen2022primer discuss learned algorithms and benchmarking, while @chen2024tutorial distinguish acceleration, solution estimation, and model adaptation. Our procedure supplies candidate assignments, but a conventional solver remains responsible for feasibility and bounds. Generalization must be evaluated at both prediction and optimization levels.

Recent studies illustrate different integration points. @qu2026 use an unsupervised scheme for parameterized mixed-integer programs and derive additional constraints from learned patterns. This differs from nonbinding partial starts, which do not remove feasible solutions. @goerigk2025 learn relevant scenarios to initialize robust combinatorial optimization; their learned object is a scenario set, not variable values. @tang2024l2o study mixed-integer nonlinear solution generation with feasibility mechanisms. None of these mechanisms implies that thresholding our network yields a feasible CFL solution. We delegate completion to Gurobi and independently validate its incumbent.

## Graph representations and solver decisions

The variable-constraint bipartite architecture of @gasse2019 is our principal architectural reference. Their task imitates strong branching; our targets are binary assignments. Architectural reuse is not replication of their branching-policy experiment. @cappart2021 review graph representations for combinatorial reasoning. Other decisions include node comparison [@labassi2022], objective prediction [@scavuzzo2024], and cutting-plane selection. In particular, @zhang2026 use structured graph learning for cut selection, rather than supervised assignment prediction. Input-order stability matters in both settings, but permutation checks cannot establish optimization quality.

Expressivity results also warrant caution. @chen2024branching identify limitations of message-passing architectures for branching scores; @chen2024quadratic examine graph representability for quadratic programs. These results motivate scrutiny but provide neither an exact-assignment guarantee nor a quadratic-programming extension for this implementation.

## Primal guidance

Prediction-based primal methods include solution-informed neighbourhood search [@ding2020], variable-bias guidance [@khalil2022], and GNN primal heuristics [@canturk2024]. Our supervision uses one independently checked solution per mathematical instance, not a distribution of near-optimal assignment biases. Neural Diving delegates partial assignments to an optimizer [@nair2020], whereas local branching restricts a neighbourhood [@fischetti2003]. Both differ from variable hints and native `Start` attributes [@gurobi2026]. The completed comparison uses partial starts only. Bound fixing, learned cuts, hints, and neighbourhood restrictions are not interchangeable treatments.

# Proposed method

## Instances and labels

For parent $p$, the preserved file defines

$$
\begin{aligned}
z_p^\star &= \min_x\; c_p^\top x+c_{p,0},\\
A_p x &\mathrel{\bowtie_p} b_p,\\
\ell_p\leq x &\leq u_p,\qquad x_j\in\mathbb Z\quad(j\in I_p).
\end{aligned}
$$

Row senses $\bowtie_p$, identities, objective constant, and domains are retained. We do not infer an unverified facility/assignment interpretation for every benchmark column. The study applies an explicit MINIMIZE override to the original MAXIMIZE headers. Original inputs and both senses are preserved in provenance. Experiments concern this disclosed minimization convention, not unchanged maximization models or an independently verified correction of every benchmark release.

Let $B_p\subseteq I_p$ be the binary support. A feasible incumbent supplies $y_{pj}\in\{0,1\}$. Admission requires finite values, identity coverage, bounds, integrality, all linear rows, objective reconstruction, and a finite terminal relative MIP gap at most 0.10. This ceiling does not certify an optimal label or eliminate alternative optima. It conditions training on solve difficulty; rejected instances remain in the evidence.

## Offline graph learning

Each variable and constraint becomes a node, with coefficient-bearing edges for nonzeros of $A_p$. Variable features comprise objective coefficient, bounds, type, and an actual Gurobi root MIPNODE relaxation value. Row features encode right-hand side and sense. Feature order, clipping, and normalization are versioned. Root values are aligned by identity; capture failure is not replaced by zeros. Gurobi is the common graph authority, including for future comparisons using SCIP-derived supervision.

The Gasse-inspired predictor uses two message-passing layers and hidden dimension 32. A versioned alternating-prenorm correction fits variable-side normalization to updated constraint messages, using training graphs only. Toy overfitting, finite-gradient, replay, and permutation tests check implementation rather than validate generalization. Training minimizes positive-class-weighted binary cross-entropy (BCE),

$$\ell_{pj}=-w_+y_{pj}\log\sigma(s_{pj})-(1-y_{pj})\log(1-\sigma(s_{pj})),$$

with $w_+$ estimated from training targets. Adam uses learning rate $10^{-3}$, norm-1 gradient clipping, seed 42, and 100 epochs. The parent-balanced sampler draws four samples per training parent per epoch. The checkpoint minimizes validation weighted BCE; its threshold maximizes validation F1. The selected threshold is $\tau=0.9991843104362488$. This high threshold does not establish calibration: class weighting and rare positives alter the decision scale.

## Class-aware partial starts

For $q_j=\sigma(s_j)$, let $\hat y_j=\mathbf1[q_j\geq\tau]$. With $n=|B_p|$, define

$$K=\min\{n,20000,\max(1,\lfloor0.10n\rfloor)\}.$$

First retain up to $K$ predicted positives in decreasing $q_j$ order. Fill the remaining support with predicted zeros in decreasing $1-q_j$ order, breaking ties by ascending variable name. Without any threshold-positive prediction, abstain rather than submit an all-zero learned start. These rules retain rare positive assignments that a single confidence ranking can displace. They do not prove feasibility, optimal ordering, or superiority to every selector.

Selected variables receive native `Start` values; others remain undefined. Objective, matrix, senses, and bounds remain unchanged, verified by a mathematical signature before and after submission. Gurobi may complete or repair the candidate. Acceptance is not proof of gap improvement. The comparator assigns ones to the largest root-LP binary values and zeros to the smallest remaining values, matching learned support and positive count without using labels. It is a conditional diagnostic comparator, not an independently selected best root-LP policy.

## Augmentation boundary

A feasible incumbent $\bar x$ can define a new model through

$$\sum_{j\in B_p:\bar x_j=0}x_j+\sum_{j\in B_p:\bar x_j=1}(1-x_j)\leq k.$$

The pipeline materializes and independently labels such descendants, with Gurobi or SCIP centres. An incumbent vector alone is not a new instance or graph. Descendants inherit parent partitions and remain training-only; they are correlated samples, not independent parents. Although implemented, **no matched four-arm learning comparison** demonstrates an augmentation benefit in the final experiment. Current results use Gurobi-labelled originals. Augmentation remains a follow-up, not an asserted cause of the gains.

# Experimental design

## Populations and information boundaries

| Stage | Parents | Permitted information | Purpose |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Fitting | 34 training originals | Admitted labels and graphs | Gradient updates and prenorm |
| Predictor selection | 10 validation originals | Labels and scores | Checkpoint and threshold |
| Predictive evaluation | 10 test originals: six easy, four medium | Held-out labels | Classification and ranking |
| Guidance qualification | Six medium validation originals | Label-free inference and optimization | Qualify fixed start policy |
| Optimization test | Six distinct medium test originals | Label-free inference and optimization | Frozen-policy comparison |

: Populations serve different purposes. Variable targets are not independent optimization replications. {#tbl-populations}

The 54-parent cohort supersedes the historical 39-parent experiment without rewriting its exclusions or results. The split manifest fixes parent roles, shared by all representations. Optimization-test parents are medium 0, 4, 7, 9, 12, and 20. The first, second, third, and fifth appear in the labelled graph-test inventory. Medium 9 and 20 are absent from it but retain their frozen test role; absence is not permission to use them for fitting or selection. Label-free inference permits their solver evaluation without importing labels.

Guidance validation uses medium 5, 6, 11, 14, 17, and 19. Its precommitted rule requires six valid, nonabstained learned starts, at least four gap wins, a nonpositive median paired difference, and at most one regression above 0.01 relative-gap units. This is development selection, not an independent confirmatory test. Optimization-test outcomes cannot reselect checkpoint, threshold, coverage, or ordering.

## Comparisons and time measurements

Each parent receives three fresh Gurobi models: control, matched root-LP start, and class-aware GNN start. Parameters are identical apart from starts: one solver thread, seed 42, 3,600-second optimization limit, and relative tolerance $10^{-4}$. Order rotates across parents, reducing systematic order confounding without constituting a randomized multi-seed design. Label-free root capture has a separate 600-second ceiling. Returned incumbents receive independent feasibility and objective checks.

For finite nonzero primal $z^P$, gap is $g=|z^P-z^D|/|z^P|$. Degenerate or unavailable values are handled explicitly. The paired effect $\Delta g_{pm}=g_{pm}-g_{p,\mathrm{control}}$ is negative when guidance helps. We report percentage-point differences, not relative percentage reductions. Native and common gaps remain distinct in receipts.

Four wall-time regions are total, data reading, model construction, and optimization. In this adapter data reading measures source verification; LP parsing belongs to model construction. Independent auditing and residual overhead are separate, so the four named measurements do not alone form an additive partition. Cold guidance includes feature preparation, inference, and worker-process cost. Reusable-artifact cost excludes already cached preparation but includes artifact verification. Offline training, queueing, and orchestration are not comparative online cost. Optimization-only reductions are not end-to-end speedups.

Budget-limited runs are right-censored for time to optimality. Failure to observe gap at most 10 percent is censored for that target, not a measured 3,600-second crossing. Callback measurements give first observed, not exact, crossing times. Paired summaries are descriptive; millions of correlated variable targets do not enlarge the six-parent solver sample.

# Results

## Prediction and learning dynamics

Predictive evaluation covers 5,536,400 targets with 5,265 positives: approximately 0.0951 percent prevalence. Pooled precision, recall, and F1 are approximately 0.6923, 0.7064, and 0.6993. ROC-AUC is 0.99969. Precision-recall area is 0.77467; average precision is reported separately rather than identified with trapezoidal area. Extreme imbalance makes accuracy and ROC-AUC inadequate stand-alone success measures. Pooled and parent-macro results answer different questions and neither certifies optimization.

![Training and validation weighted BCE on the same axes for the actual 100-epoch, 54-parent experiment. The immutable history is not reconstructed from the earlier easy-only run.](figures/figure_training_validation_loss.pdf){#fig-loss width=95%}

{{< include tables/current_predictive.qmd >}}

Training weighted BCE decreases from 1.5877 to 0.0275. Validation BCE reaches its minimum of 0.0510 at epoch 34, then rises to 0.1124 at epoch 100; the final epoch is not the selected checkpoint. This pattern cautions against interpreting continued training-loss reduction as improved generalization. Loss curves do not establish calibration. Brier score and calibration diagnostics are retained, but weighting and label selection require further study. This cohort establishes neither unseen-hard prediction nor multi-family transfer.

## Negative pilot and validation

An earlier easy-only predictor and simpler selector had mixed medium outcomes: gap improved from about 6.753 to 6.391 percent on medium 0 but worsened from 7.172 to 7.830 percent on medium 1. Both exhausted the budget and guided total cost increased. That pilot motivates class-aware selection but is not a controlled selector ablation because training population also changed.

The six-parent guidance validation produced four gap wins and a median difference of -1.224 points. Medium 11 regressed by 2.326 points and medium 17 by 0.735 points. Medium 19 attained zero terminal gap after approximately 671 seconds while control remained budget-limited. The rule passed; unfavorable cases remain relevant to reliability.

## Frozen optimization test

{{< include tables/current_heldout.qmd >}}

Learned starts improve terminal gap on five of six test parents, with median difference -1.164 points. Medium 0 regresses in terminal gap despite an earlier 10-percent crossing; medium 4 has a slightly better gap but a later crossing. Four learned runs observe gap at most 10 percent versus three control and three root-LP runs. Four learned runs and all six runs of each comparator are censored for time to optimality. Near-equal budget-limited times are not speedups. Earlier completions on two learned runs are instance-specific, not a general time-to-optimality ratio against censored controls.

![Validation and optimization-test terminal-gap effects. Negative values favor the learned start. Qualification and test observations are shown separately.](figures/figure_validation_test_gap_effects.pdf){#fig-effects width=95%}

![First observed optimization time to gap at most 10 percent. Unobserved crossings remain censored; feature preparation and inference are additional online costs.](figures/figure_time_to_ten_percent_gap.pdf){#fig-target-time width=95%}

## Influence and computational cost

{{< include tables/current_influence.qmd >}}

Mean improvement is driven by medium 20 and 12. Excluding both leaves a favorable direction but substantially smaller magnitude. These exclusions are post-analysis diagnostics, not alternative frozen cohorts or new selection criteria. They do not justify discarding observations or a robust population-effect claim. The root-LP comparator wins on one of six parents and has a positive median difference of about 1.124 points against control. Its dependence on learned class composition limits causal interpretation.

{{< include tables/current_timing.qmd >}}

Cold cost includes preparation and inference. Cached features represent a different use case, not a free cold start. The transferred publication tables contain worker total and optimization time, but not the individual reading, construction, preparation, or inference measurements. Those components are recorded upstream; they are not reconstructed or treated as zero here. Consequently, these tables alone cannot quantify cold end-to-end acceleration. Observed expansion and training costs are not claimed to equal the complete cumulative cost of the research.

# Discussion and limitations

The results separate three propositions: assignments are learnable on admitted graphs; the specified policy passed validation qualification; and the frozen medium test displays a favorable gap pattern. They do not imply statistical significance, an optimal-assignment predictor, or reliable benefit on every instance. Accepted starts and ROC-AUC alone are insufficient.

Label admission can underrepresent difficult instances and retains approximate solutions with alternative optima. Prediction can disagree with a label without harming feasibility or objective quality. Two optimization-test parents lack admitted predictive labels, further distinguishing the evaluations. One seed, six test parents, an influence-sensitive mean, and policy development after a negative pilot limit inference. Validation controls subsequent test reuse but does not retrospectively preregister the entire development history.

There is no calibrated-probability claim or independent random-support ablation. The matched root-LP comparator is conditional on learned support. Rotated method order and fixed parameters do not remove system variability. Censoring prevents naive time-to-optimality averages, and preparation can offset optimization benefits. High variable-level metric precision is not parent-level uncertainty.

The full 90-parent target, hard-instance warm-start demonstration, and final augmentation comparison remain unachieved. Examined longer hard solves failed the label-quality ceiling; they were not shown mathematically infeasible. Implemented capabilities and engineering checks are not completed scientific experiments.

# Conclusions and future work

Quality-screened bipartite learning can provide partial starts with a favorable descriptive terminal-gap pattern on the examined medium test parents. Class-aware selection retains scarce predicted positives without changing the model. The median favors learning, but regressions, censoring, influence sensitivity, and online overhead prevent general acceleration claims.

Replication should use new frozen seeds and parent-level uncertainty without retuning on the current test. Controlled studies should isolate support ordering, class composition, calibration, and training population; add independent root-LP and random-support baselines; and compare original-only learning with independently labelled Gurobi- and SCIP-centred descendants at equal parent sampling mass and optimizer-step budgets. Descendants cannot replace independent parent coverage. Extension to 90 originals requires medium/hard budget and resource experiments that preserve unsuccessful attempts.

Further work includes bipartite community and role analysis and visualization beyond PCA/UMAP. Projections are not automatically learned embeddings or explanations. A curated Zenodo release should version intermediate models, graphs, actually produced embeddings, and principal results after redistribution-rights review. Neither a draft nor a planned DOI constitutes published availability.

# Reproducibility and availability

The [canonical repository](https://github.com/unb-lamfo-or-ai-hpc/cfl-gurobi-gnn) provides source, split manifest, protocols, requirements, and build instructions. The supplementary ledger binds current CSVs and figures by SHA256 to training, validation, and test evidence. Historical 39-parent materials are retained separately, not used for the current loss figure. Publication builds perform no training, inference, or solver execution. Dependency ranges are not claimed to be a fully resolved lock.

## Computational environment

Experiments used UJA DGX-DaSCI at the Higher Polytechnic School of Jaén, University of Jaén. The supplied DGX-1 inventory lists eight 32-GB Tesla V100 GPUs, two 20-core x86 CPUs at 2.2 GHz, and 512 GB memory. This is a machine inventory, **not a runtime hardware probe**, and does not establish that a training run uses all eight GPUs. Recorded solver workers use one Gurobi thread despite larger Slurm CPU allocations. Run resources and software versions belong to individual receipts, not hardware capacity. The storage inventory includes an OS SATA SSD with a 6 Gb/s interface and a four-device SSD RAID-0 array; interface rate is not measured throughput. Missing values will remain explicitly unavailable rather than invented.

## Data availability and licensing

Original instances are distributed through [MILPBench](https://github.com/thuiar/MILPBench). Code and original manuscript material use the MIT License, without relicensing benchmark inputs, solvers, or publisher templates. Versioned shareable evidence excludes raw logs, license material, private paths, and checkpoints. No published Zenodo DOI is verified. Full intermediate/graph redistribution remains subject to provenance and rights review; archive availability and the submission data statement require author completion before submission. This limitation is not replaced with a claim of complete raw-data deposition.
